claim: Bacterial meningitis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, especially among infants and the elderly.
source: Bacterial meningitis is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, especially among infants and the elderly.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established medical knowledge about bacterial meningitis.

claim: Upon infection, the major meningeal cell types – including endothelial cells (ECs), macrophages, and fibroblasts – exhibit distinctive changes in their transcriptomes.
source: Upon infection, the major meningeal cell types – including endothelial cells (ECs), macrophages, and fibroblasts – exhibit distinctive changes in their transcriptomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNAseq data presented in the manuscript showing transcriptome changes across cell types.

claim: ECs in the leptomeninges redistribute CLDN5 and PECAM1 upon infection.
source: Additionally, ECs in the leptomeninges redistribute CLDN5 and PECAM1, and leptomeningeal capillaries exhibit foci with reduced blood-brain barrier integrity.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-B demonstrating redistribution of these proteins.

claim: Leptomeningeal capillaries exhibit foci with reduced blood-brain barrier integrity upon infection.
source: Additionally, ECs in the leptomeninges redistribute CLDN5 and PECAM1, and leptomeningeal capillaries exhibit foci with reduced blood-brain barrier integrity.
evidence: This is supported by Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage data shown in Figures 5A-C.

claim: The vascular response to infection appears to be largely driven by TLR4 signaling.
source: The vascular response to infection appears to be largely driven by TLR4 signaling, as determined by the nearly identical responses induced by infection and LPS administration and by the blunted response to infection in Tlr4-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing LPS treatment to E. coli infection and by experiments with Tlr4-/- mice shown in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Infection and LPS administration induce nearly identical vascular responses.
source: The vascular response to infection appears to be largely driven by TLR4 signaling, as determined by the nearly identical responses induced by infection and LPS administration and by the blunted response to infection in Tlr4-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Tlr4-/- mice show a blunted vascular response to infection.
source: The vascular response to infection appears to be largely driven by TLR4 signaling, as determined by the nearly identical responses induced by infection and LPS administration and by the blunted response to infection in Tlr4-/- mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Knocking out Ccr2 had little or no effect on the response of leptomeningeal ECs to E. coli infection.
source: Interestingly, knocking out Ccr2, encoding a major chemoattractant for monocytes, or acute depletion of leptomeningeal macrophages, following intracebroventricular injection of liposomal clodronate, had little or no effect on the response of leptomeningeal ECs to E. coli infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Ccr2-/- mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: Acute depletion of leptomeningeal macrophages following intracerebroventricular injection of liposomal clodronate had little or no effect on the response of leptomeningeal ECs to E. coli infection.
source: Interestingly, knocking out Ccr2, encoding a major chemoattractant for monocytes, or acute depletion of leptomeningeal macrophages, following intracebroventricular injection of liposomal clodronate, had little or no effect on the response of leptomeningeal ECs to E. coli infection.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: EC responses to infection are largely driven by the intrinsic EC response to LPS.
source: Taken together, these data imply that EC responses to infection are largely driven by the intrinsic EC response to LPS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of LPS treatment, Tlr4-/- experiments, and macrophage depletion experiments.

claim: The meninges consists of the pia, sub-arachnoid space, arachnoid, and dura.
source: Starting from the surface of the brain and moving toward the skin, the meninges consists of: (1) the pia, a thin and semi-permeable layer of cells that allows passage of small molecules and proteins between the CNS parenchyma and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF); (2) the sub-arachnoid space, a highly vascularized region containing fibroblasts and immune cells that is filled with CSF and supported by a web of trabeculae; (3) the arachnoid, including an outer epithelial barrier layer that serves as the outer boundary of the CSF-accessible space; and (4) the dura, a fibrous layer containing draining sinuses (veins), lymphatics, fibroblasts, and immune cells.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about meningeal structure, also supported by citations (Coles et al., 2017a; Weller et al., 2018).

claim: The pia is a thin and semi-permeable layer of cells that allows passage of small molecules and proteins between the CNS parenchyma and the cerebrospinal fluid.
source: (1) the pia, a thin and semi-permeable layer of cells that allows passage of small molecules and proteins between the CNS parenchyma and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about the pia mater.

claim: Layers 1–3 together comprise the leptomeninges.
source: Layers 1–3 together comprise the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about meningeal organization.

claim: The meninges hosts a diverse collection of immune cells, including macrophages, monocytes, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), T-cells, B-cells, dendritic cells, and mast cells.
source: The meninges hosts a diverse collection of immune cells, including macrophages [referred to as barrier-associated macrophages (BAMs) or CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs)], monocytes, innate lymphoid cells (ILCs), T-cells, B-cells, dendritic cells, and mast cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and immuno-phenotyping have revealed distinctive layer-specific types and abundances of immune cells in the meninges.
source: Recent single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) and immuno-phenotyping have revealed distinctive layer-specific types and abundances of these immune cells (Rua and McGavern, 2018; Alves de Lima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Macrophages can be divided into several molecularly distinct classes that are characterized by different half-lives and capacities for self-renewal.
source: Macrophages are especially abundant, and they can be divided into several molecularly distinct classes that are characterized by different half-lives and capacities for self-renewal (Mrdjen et al., 2018; Kierdorf et al., 2019; Van Hove et al., 2019; Masuda et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Layer specific diversity is observed among meningeal fibroblasts, with molecularly distinctive pial, arachnoid, and perivascular fibroblasts, as well as two types of dural fibroblasts.
source: Layer specific diversity is also observed among meningeal fibroblasts, with molecularly distinctive pial, arachnoid, and perivascular fibroblasts, as well as two types of dural fibroblasts (DeSisto et al., 2020; Derk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A wide variety of CNS injuries and disease processes involve the meninges, including stroke, traumatic brain injury, neuroinflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis, neurodegenerative diseases, and infections.
source: A wide variety of CNS injuries and disease processes involve the meninges, including stroke, traumatic brain injury, neuroinflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis, neurodegenerative diseases, and infections (Derk et al., 2021; Alves de Lima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mouse models of stroke, genetic ablation of meningeal mast cells reduces infarct size and brain swelling.
source: For example, in mouse models of stroke, genetic ablation of meningeal mast cells reduces infarct size and brain swelling (Arac et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published experimental work.

claim: Bacterial meningitis is most common among young children and the elderly.
source: Bacterial meningitis is most common among young children and the elderly, and it is generally initiated by a blood-borne infection (Ku et al., 2015; McGill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established epidemiological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Bacterial meningitis is generally initiated by a blood-borne infection.
source: Bacterial meningitis is most common among young children and the elderly, and it is generally initiated by a blood-borne infection (Ku et al., 2015; McGill et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The annual incidence of bacterial meningitis ranges from ~2 per 100,000 people in Western Europe and North America to 100–1000 per 100,000 people in the Sahel region of Africa.
source: The annual incidence of bacterial meningitis ranges from ~2 per 100,000 people in Western Europe and North America to 100–1000 per 100,000 people in the Sahel region of Africa (Ku et al., 2015; GBD 2016 Meningitis Collaborators, 2018).
evidence: This is epidemiological data supported by citations.

claim: In Western Europe and North America, mortality from bacterial meningitis is 10–20%, with >30% of survivors experiencing residual neurologic defects.
source: In Western Europe and North America, mortality from bacterial meningitis is 10–20%, with >30% of survivors experiencing residual neurologic defects (McGill et al., 2016; Eisen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is epidemiological data supported by citations.

claim: Meningitis in the neonatal period typically results from bacterial infection during or immediately prior to delivery.
source: Meningitis in the neonatal period, when the immune system is immature, typically results from bacterial infection during or immediately prior to delivery.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about neonatal meningitis.

claim: Bacteria, most commonly Group B Streptococci and E. coli, are introduced into the bloodstream through breaks in the infant's skin or via intra-amniotic infection.
source: Bacteria, most commonly Group B Streptococci and E. coli, are introduced into the bloodstream through breaks in the infant's skin or via intra-amniotic infection (Gaschignard et al., 2011; Shane et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established medical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The incidence of bacterial meningitis in neonates is ~0.3 per 1000 live births in developed countries and ~4 per 1000 live births in less developed countries.
source: The incidence of bacterial meningitis in neonates is ~0.3 per 1000 live births in developed countries and ~4 per 1000 live births in less developed countries (Ku et al., 2015).
evidence: This is epidemiological data supported by a citation.

claim: Among survivors of neonatal meningitis, 20–70% are left with long-lasting neurologic sequelae, including hearing loss, epilepsy, and learning and/or behavioral disabilities.
source: Among survivors of neonatal meningitis, 20–70% (the number depending on the country) are left with long-lasting neurologic sequelae, including hearing loss, epilepsy, and learning and/or behavioral disabilities (Peltola et al., 2021).
evidence: This is epidemiological data supported by a citation.

claim: When the skull and brain are separated in the absence of fixation, the natural cleavage plane is between the leptomeninges and dura.
source: When the skull and brain are separated in the absence of fixation, the natural cleavage plane is between the leptomeninges and dura (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the dissection protocol described in the manuscript.

claim: The separation of the unfixed leptomeninges from the brain parenchyma works best with tissue from young mice: it is efficient with tissue harvested at postnatal day (P)6 but fails with adult tissue.
source: In our hands, the separation of the unfixed leptomeninges from the brain parenchyma works best with tissue from young mice: it is efficient with tissue harvested at postnatal day (P)6 but, as noted by Van Hove et al., 2019 and confirmed by us, it fails with adult tissue.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the manuscript, also supported by a citation.

claim: Leptomeningeal ECs, but not dura ECs, express GLUT1, a blood-brain barrier (BBB) marker.
source: Leptomeningeal ECs, but not dura ECs, express GLUT1, a blood-brain barrier (BBB) marker (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fourteen principal cell clusters were identified with Seurat.
source: Fourteen principal cell clusters were identified with Seurat, and their identities were assigned by immunostaining and with reference to published data, as seen in the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) plots in Figure 1F and H (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Five large clusters represent fibroblasts – one pial, one arachnoid, and three dural.
source: Strikingly, five large clusters represent fibroblasts – one pial, one arachnoid, and three dural, as determined by a comparison with published data on meningeal fibroblasts (DeSisto et al., 2020; Derk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq analysis, supported by comparison to published data.

claim: Comparing UMAP plots of control and infected datasets reveals shifts in the positions of the immune cell and fibroblast clusters with infection.
source: Comparing UMAP plots of control and infected datasets reveals shifts in the positions of the immune cell and fibroblast clusters with infection (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: E. coli strain RFP-RS218 (O18:K1:H7) is a clinical isolate from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of a neonate with meningitis.
source: E. coli strain RFP-RS218 (O18:K1:H7). This strain is a clinical isolate from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of a neonate with meningitis and it has been derivatized by the addition of a plasmid expressing red fluorescent protein (RFP) to facilitate visualization of E. coli cells in tissue.
evidence: This is information about the bacterial strain used, supported by a citation (Zhu et al., 2020).

claim: P5 was chosen as the age of inoculation to approximate the degree of maturity of the neonatal human immune system.
source: P5 was chosen as the age of inoculation to approximate the degree of maturity of the neonatal human immune system (Holsapple et al., 2003; Kuper et al., 2016; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations comparing mouse and human immune system development.

claim: One day after E. coli inoculation, the mice appeared lethargic and they stopped gaining weight.
source: One day after E. coli inoculation, the mice appeared lethargic and they stopped gaining weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the infection model, supported by weight data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Any inoculated mice that were not sacrificed died within two days of the inoculation.
source: Any inoculated mice that were not sacrificed died within two days of the inoculation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the infection model, supported by survival data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: At sacrifice, 22 hr after subcutaneous inoculation, E. coli cells were typically observed in a patchy distribution in the leptomeninges and dura, and at much sparser density within the brain.
source: At sacrifice, 22 hr after subcutaneous inoculation, E. coli cells were typically observed in a patchy distribution in the leptomeninges and dura, and at much sparser density within the brain (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the infection model, supported by imaging data in Figure 2A-D.

claim: The number of E. coli per unit area in flatmounts of the dura sinus region was, on average, ~20-fold greater than the number of E. coli in the same area in flatmounts of the leptomeninges.
source: The number of E. coli per unit area in flatmounts of the dura sinus region was, on average, ~20-fold greater than the number of E. coli in the same area in flatmounts of the leptomeninges, reflecting, in part, the several fold greater depth of the dura sinus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, left plot).
evidence: This is a quantification from the infection model shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The density of macrophages in the leptomeninges increased by only ~20% upon infection.
source: Despite the presence of E. coli, the density of macrophages in the leptomeninges, which are normally present at 1500–2000 cells per mm2, increased by only ~20% (Figure 2E; for all image quantifications, the number of mice in each sample are listed in Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Macrophage morphology changed dramatically with infection, from small and rounded to large and irregularly shaped.
source: However, macrophage morphology changed dramatically with infection, from small and rounded to large and irregularly shaped (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Infection led to a reduction in LYVE1 abundance in macrophages.
source: Infection also led to a reduction in LYVE1 abundance, but little or no change in CD180 or CD206 abundance, in macrophages (Figure 2F, G and I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: Infection led to little or no change in CD180 or CD206 abundance in macrophages.
source: Infection also led to a reduction in LYVE1 abundance, but little or no change in CD180 or CD206 abundance, in macrophages (Figure 2F, G and I).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2F-G and quantified in Figure 2I.

claim: In the dura of infected mice, IL6 was induced in fibroblasts.
source: In the dura of infected mice, IL6 was induced in fibroblasts, with the cell type assignment determined by the observed increase in fibroblast-specific Il6 transcript abundance in the snRNAseq datasets (Figure 2H and I, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 2H-I and snRNAseq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In both the dura and leptomeninges, the number of cells expressing S100A8 increased ~10-fold upon infection.
source: In both the dura and leptomeninges, the number of cells expressing S100A8, a marker for monocytes and immature macrophages, increased ~10-fold (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J-K.

claim: Scatter plots encompassing all transcripts reveal relatively few changes in the contaminating neuron and glia clusters and many more changes in each of the principal meningeal clusters.
source: In comparing control vs. infected datasets for each of the principal cell clusters, scatter plots encompassing all transcripts reveal relatively few changes in the contaminating neuron and glia clusters and many more changes in each of the principal meningeal clusters, with roughly equal numbers of up- and down-regulated transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Hierarchical clustering in a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) shows prominent induction of inflammatory responses across all meningeal cell types.
source: Hierarchical clustering in a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) with control vs. infected samples shows prominent induction of inflammatory responses ('complement', 'interferon gamma response', 'IL6 JAK STAT3 signaling', 'TNFA signaling via NFKB') across all meningeal cell types.
evidence: This is a result from GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: ECs and arachnoid barrier cells show a reduction in apical barrier (i.e. tight junction) transcripts, but this reduction did not reach statistical significance.
source: ECs and arachnoid barrier cells show a reduction in apical barrier (i.e. tight junction) transcripts, but this reduction did not reach statistical significance (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The relative abundances of the principal meningeal cell types did not change with infection, as judged by counting nuclei in the five snRNAseq libraries.
source: Although the relative abundances of the principal meningeal cell types did not change with infection, as judged by counting nuclei in the five snRNAseq libraries (Figure 3D upper panel), parsing the individual immune cell types revealed an ~twofold decrease in the abundance of CCL2- resident macrophages, a > 10-fold increase in inflammatory macrophages (IL1R1+ and IL1R1-), and a several-fold increase in the abundance of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells (Figure 3D, lower panel).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Parsing the individual immune cell types revealed an ~twofold decrease in the abundance of CCL2- resident macrophages with infection.
source: Although the relative abundances of the principal meningeal cell types did not change with infection, as judged by counting nuclei in the five snRNAseq libraries (Figure 3D upper panel), parsing the individual immune cell types revealed an ~twofold decrease in the abundance of CCL2- resident macrophages, a > 10-fold increase in inflammatory macrophages (IL1R1+ and IL1R1-), and a several-fold increase in the abundance of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells (Figure 3D, lower panel).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Parsing the individual immune cell types revealed a > 10-fold increase in inflammatory macrophages (IL1R1+ and IL1R1-) with infection.
source: Although the relative abundances of the principal meningeal cell types did not change with infection, as judged by counting nuclei in the five snRNAseq libraries (Figure 3D upper panel), parsing the individual immune cell types revealed an ~twofold decrease in the abundance of CCL2- resident macrophages, a > 10-fold increase in inflammatory macrophages (IL1R1+ and IL1R1-), and a several-fold increase in the abundance of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells (Figure 3D, lower panel).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Parsing the individual immune cell types revealed a several-fold increase in the abundance of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells with infection.
source: Although the relative abundances of the principal meningeal cell types did not change with infection, as judged by counting nuclei in the five snRNAseq libraries (Figure 3D upper panel), parsing the individual immune cell types revealed an ~twofold decrease in the abundance of CCL2- resident macrophages, a > 10-fold increase in inflammatory macrophages (IL1R1+ and IL1R1-), and a several-fold increase in the abundance of monocytes or monocyte-derived cells (Figure 3D, lower panel).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Among genes that are either up- or down-regulated in CCL2- or CCL2+ resident macrophages, several dozen show greater than 5-fold changes in abundance.
source: Among genes that are either up- or down-regulated in CCL2- or CCL2+ resident macrophages, several dozen show greater than 5-fold changes in abundance (Figure 3E and Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CCL2- and CCL2+ macrophages show nearly identical changes among the transcripts with the greatest increases in abundance with infection.
source: As seen in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, CCL2- and CCL2+ macrophages show nearly identical changes among the transcripts with the greatest increases in abundance with infection, and somewhat greater variability among transcripts with the greatest decreases in abundance with infection.
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CD180 levels showed little change at 22 hr post-infection by immunostaining, suggestive of a long protein half-life.
source: Interestingly, by immunostaining, CD180 levels showed little change at this time point (22 hr post-infection; Figure 2G and I), suggestive of a long protein half-life, whereas LYVE1 levels showed a large reduction (Figure 2F and I), suggestive of post-transcriptional as well as transcriptional down-regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing transcript and protein levels from snRNAseq and immunostaining data.

claim: LYVE1 levels showed a large reduction by immunostaining, suggestive of post-transcriptional as well as transcriptional down-regulation.
source: Interestingly, by immunostaining, CD180 levels showed little change at this time point (22 hr post-infection; Figure 2G and I), suggestive of a long protein half-life, whereas LYVE1 levels showed a large reduction (Figure 2F and I), suggestive of post-transcriptional as well as transcriptional down-regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing transcript and protein levels from snRNAseq and immunostaining data.

claim: Among the 50 members of the collagen gene family, 25 show detectable expression in the meninges by snRNAseq and 19/25 are down-regulated but only 2/25 are up-regulated.
source: Transcripts coding for multiple collagen subtypes are down-regulated by infection: among the 50 members of the collagen gene family, 25 show detectable expression in the meninges by snRNAseq and 19/25 are down-regulated but only 2/25 are up-regulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Of the ~350 members of the mouse Slc gene family with detectable expression in meningeal cells, 37 show infection-dependent changes in transcript abundance in one or more meningeal cell types by snRNAseq, with 21/37 down-regulated and 6/37 up-regulated by log2-fold>0.25 following infection.
source: Similarly, multiple transcripts coding for SLC transporters are down-regulated in meningeal fibroblasts. Of the ~350 members of the mouse Slc gene family with detectable expression in meningeal cells, 37 show infection-dependent changes in transcript abundance in one or more meningeal cell types by snRNAseq, with 21/37 down-regulated and 6/37 up-regulated by log2-fold>0.25 following infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Slc39a14, which codes for a divalent metal transporter, is unusual in its substantial up-regulation with infection.
source: Slc39a14, which codes for a divalent metal transporter, is unusual in its substantial up-regulation with infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Infection leads to an expansion in the size of the leptomeninges and dura EC clusters, indicative of increased heterogeneity in transcriptome content.
source: Infection leads to an expansion in the size of the leptomeninges and dura EC clusters (Figure 4A and E), indicative of increased heterogeneity in transcriptome content, with little or no change in the proportions of the different EC subtypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq UMAP analysis shown in Figure 4A and E.

claim: Infection produces little or no change in the proportions of the different EC subtypes.
source: Infection leads to an expansion in the size of the leptomeninges and dura EC clusters (Figure 4A and E), indicative of increased heterogeneity in transcriptome content, with little or no change in the proportions of the different EC subtypes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantification from the snRNAseq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Transcripts coding for amino acid transporters SLC7A1 and SLC7A5 are down-regulated in leptomeningeal ECs upon infection.
source: Multiple transcriptome changes distinguish the infection responses of different EC clusters, including down-regulation of transcripts coding for amino acid transporters SLC7A1 and SLC7A5 in leptomeningeal ECs and down-regulation of transcripts coding for plasmalemma vesicle associated protein (PLVAP; a marker of high permeability vasculature) and the mechanosensory channel PIEZO2 in dural ECs (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Transcripts coding for PLVAP and PIEZO2 are down-regulated in dural ECs upon infection.
source: Multiple transcriptome changes distinguish the infection responses of different EC clusters, including down-regulation of transcripts coding for amino acid transporters SLC7A1 and SLC7A5 in leptomeningeal ECs and down-regulation of transcripts coding for plasmalemma vesicle associated protein (PLVAP; a marker of high permeability vasculature) and the mechanosensory channel PIEZO2 in dural ECs (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Transcripts coding for VEGFR2/KDR are down-regulated in leptomeningeal and dural ECs upon infection.
source: Transcripts coding for VEGFR2/KDR are down-regulated in leptomeningeal and dural ECs (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from the snRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: In leptomeninges flatmounts, infection produces mislocalization and clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1.
source: In leptomeninges flatmounts, infection produces mislocalization and clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1, disorganized capillary morphology, and an expansion of the area covered by capillaries (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Infection produces disorganized capillary morphology in leptomeninges flatmounts.
source: In leptomeninges flatmounts, infection produces mislocalization and clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1, disorganized capillary morphology, and an expansion of the area covered by capillaries (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Infection produces an expansion of the area covered by capillaries in leptomeninges flatmounts.
source: In leptomeninges flatmounts, infection produces mislocalization and clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1, disorganized capillary morphology, and an expansion of the area covered by capillaries (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Immunoblotting of leptomeningeal proteins shows a modest reduction in the mean level of CLDN5, but this trend did not reach statistical significance.
source: Immunoblotting of leptomeningeal proteins shows a modest reduction in the mean level of CLDN5, but this trend did not reach statistical significance due to the relatively high animal-to-animal variability in the infected group (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There are patchy deficiencies in vascular barrier integrity following infection, with a spatial distribution that closely matches the clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1, as revealed by extravasation of Sulfo-NHS-biotin.
source: Functionally, there are patchy deficiencies in vascular barrier integrity following infection, with a spatial distribution that closely matches the clustering of CLDN5 and PECAM1, as revealed by extravasation of Sulfo-NHS-biotin, a low molecular weight intravascular tracer (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage experiments shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The same infection-associated vascular phenotypes were also seen one day after an intraperitoneal (IP) injection of 10 mg/kg lipopolysaccharide (LPS).
source: The same infection-associated vascular phenotypes were also seen one day after an intraperitoneal (IP) injection of 10 mg/kg lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a potent activator of the innate immune response to gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from LPS treatment experiments shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: VEGFR2 immunostaining is greatly reduced in the leptomeninges upon infection.
source: Consistent with the down-regulation of Vegfr2/Kdr transcripts seen in infected ECs by snRNAseq (Figure 4C–E), VEGFR2 immunostaining is also greatly reduced in the leptomeninges (Figure 5E and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E and quantified in Figure 5H.

claim: The enhanced vascular permeability associated with bacterial infection is not caused by increased VEGF signaling.
source: As VEGFR2 is the principal receptor for VEGF signaling in ECs, its down-regulation suggests that the enhanced vascular permeability associated with bacterial infection is not caused by increased VEGF signaling, a known mechanism for increasing vascular permeability (Senger et al., 1983; Roberts and Palade, 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed down-regulation of VEGFR2 and established knowledge about VEGF signaling.

claim: In control leptomeninges flatmounts, LEF1 accumulates in vein and capillary EC nuclei with minimal accumulation in arterial ECs.
source: In control leptomeninges flatmounts, LEF1 accumulates in vein and capillary EC nuclei with minimal accumulation in arterial ECs (Figure 5F, left panels).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In infected leptomeninges flatmounts, LEF1 immunostaining in ECs is greatly reduced, but it persists in many non-ECs.
source: Strikingly, in infected leptomeninges flatmounts, LEF1 immunostaining in ECs is greatly reduced, but it persists in many non-ECs (Figure 5F, right panels; and Figure 5H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F and quantified in Figure 5H.

claim: By immunoblotting, total leptomeningeal LEF1 levels are reduced by ~25%, a change that was not statistically significant.
source: By immunoblotting, total leptomeningeal LEF1 levels are reduced by ~25%, a change that was not statistically significant (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a result from immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: With infection, a reduction is seen in CLDN5 and PECAM1 specifically in leptomeningeal veins.
source: The right panels of Figure 5F shows reductions in CLDN5 and PECAM1 specifically in leptomeningeal veins, which appear as 'shadows' in the flatmount images.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: With infection, a reduction is seen for ERG, a pan EC transcription factor.
source: With infection, a reduction is also seen for ERG, a pan EC transcription factor (Figure 5F and H).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F and quantified in Figure 5H.

claim: Infection leads to reduced BBB integrity in the leptomeningeal vasculature, at least in part, by reducing WNT signaling in ECs.
source: These data are consistent with a model in which infection leads to reduced BBB integrity in the leptomeningeal vasculature, at least in part, by reducing WNT signaling in ECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in LEF1 and established knowledge about WNT signaling in BBB maintenance.

claim: With infection, the alignment of elongated EC nuclei with the long axis of dural veins is diminished.
source: Venous ECs throughout the body typically exhibit elongated nuclei that are aligned with the long axis of the vein, and therefore also with the direction of blood flow. With infection, this alignment is diminished in dural veins (Figure 6A and B), suggesting a general effect of infection on cytoskeletal organization within venous ECs.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Infection has a general effect on cytoskeletal organization within venous ECs.
source: With infection, this alignment is diminished in dural veins (Figure 6A and B), suggesting a general effect of infection on cytoskeletal organization within venous ECs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in nuclear alignment.

claim: In both dura and leptomeninges, NF kappaB reporter expression was induced by infection almost exclusively in ECs.
source: In both dura and leptomeninges, NF kappaB reporter expression was induced by infection almost exclusively in ECs, with reporter positive EC nuclei increasing from ~1% to~20% in the dura and from ~1% to~5% in the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Reporter positive EC nuclei increased from ~1% to ~20% in the dura upon infection.
source: In both dura and leptomeninges, NF kappaB reporter expression was induced by infection almost exclusively in ECs, with reporter positive EC nuclei increasing from ~1% to~20% in the dura and from ~1% to~5% in the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Reporter positive EC nuclei increased from ~1% to ~5% in the leptomeninges upon infection.
source: In both dura and leptomeninges, NF kappaB reporter expression was induced by infection almost exclusively in ECs, with reporter positive EC nuclei increasing from ~1% to~20% in the dura and from ~1% to~5% in the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: There is substantial cell-to-cell heterogeneity in meningeal EC responses to infection.
source: A second surprising feature was the cell-to-cell heterogeneity in EC expression, with reporter expressing ECs adjacent to non-expressing ECs in an apparently random pattern. The latter observation suggests substantial cell-to-cell heterogeneity in meningeal EC responses to infection, consistent with the observed broadening of infected EC clusters in the UMAP plots in Figure 4A and E.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed heterogeneity in NF kappaB reporter expression and UMAP cluster broadening.

claim: At one day post-infection, the number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts did not differ significantly between C57 WT control and Ccr2-/- mice.
source: At one day post-infection, the number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts did not differ significantly between C57 WT control and Ccr2-/- mice, whereas the number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts was increased ~twofold in Tlr4-/- mice, albeit with substantial scatter in the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, center plot).
evidence: This is a quantification from bacterial counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts was increased ~twofold in Tlr4-/- mice at one day post-infection.
source: At one day post-infection, the number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts did not differ significantly between C57 WT control and Ccr2-/- mice, whereas the number of E. coli in leptomeninges flatmounts was increased ~twofold in Tlr4-/- mice, albeit with substantial scatter in the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, center plot).
evidence: This is a quantification from bacterial counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The leptomeningeal vasculature of Tlr4-/- mice showed minimal changes in the distribution of CLDN5 and very few regions of Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage in response to infection.
source: In response to infection, the leptomeningeal vasculature of Tlr4-/- mice showed minimal changes in the distribution of CLDN5 and very few regions of Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Ccr2-/- mice showed a clumpy redistribution of CLDN5 and localized regions of Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage in response to infection, much like the C57BL/6 J WT control.
source: In contrast, Ccr2-/- mice showed a clumpy redistribution of CLDN5 and localized regions of Sulfo-NHS-biotin leakage, much like the C57BL/6 J WT control (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In control (i.e., uninfected) Tlr4-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages was ~65% of the WT value.
source: In control (i.e., uninfected) Tlr4-/- and Ccr2-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages (as quantified by PU.1 immunostaining) was, respectively,~65% and~90% of the WT value, and this density rose by ~50% in infected Tlr4-/- mice, but showed little or no change in infected Ccr2-/- or C57 WT mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In control (i.e., uninfected) Ccr2-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages was ~90% of the WT value.
source: In control (i.e., uninfected) Tlr4-/- and Ccr2-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages (as quantified by PU.1 immunostaining) was, respectively,~65% and~90% of the WT value, and this density rose by ~50% in infected Tlr4-/- mice, but showed little or no change in infected Ccr2-/- or C57 WT mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Macrophage density rose by ~50% in infected Tlr4-/- mice.
source: In control (i.e., uninfected) Tlr4-/- and Ccr2-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages (as quantified by PU.1 immunostaining) was, respectively,~65% and~90% of the WT value, and this density rose by ~50% in infected Tlr4-/- mice, but showed little or no change in infected Ccr2-/- or C57 WT mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Macrophage density showed little or no change in infected Ccr2-/- or C57 WT mice.
source: In control (i.e., uninfected) Tlr4-/- and Ccr2-/- mice, the density of leptomeningeal macrophages (as quantified by PU.1 immunostaining) was, respectively,~65% and~90% of the WT value, and this density rose by ~50% in infected Tlr4-/- mice, but showed little or no change in infected Ccr2-/- or C57 WT mice (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantification from immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The lower baseline number of macrophages in the Tlr4-/- leptomeninges compared to WT could reflect a modestly higher level of macrophage proliferation in the WT driven by a basal level of constitutive TLR4 signaling.
source: The lower baseline number of macrophages in the Tlr4-/- leptomeninges compared to WT could reflect a modestly higher level of macrophage proliferation in the WT driven by a basal level of constitutive TLR4 signaling, perhaps in response to LPS from the developing gut and/or skin microbiomes or from adult feces in the cage.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed difference in baseline macrophage numbers.

claim: The lower baseline number of macrophages in the Ccr2-/- leptomeninges compared to WT could reflect reduced monocyte ingress.
source: The lower baseline number of macrophages in the Ccr2-/- leptomeninges compared to WT could reflect reduced monocyte ingress.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed difference in baseline macrophage numbers.

claim: The number of E. coli in the leptomeninges did not differ significantly between mice that received control vs. clodronate liposomes.
source: The number of E. coli in the leptomeninges did not differ significantly between mice that received control vs. clodronate liposomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, right plot).
evidence: This is a quantification from bacterial counting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the infection-dependent redistribution of CLDN5 in leptomeningeal ECs.
source: Surprisingly, eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the infection-dependent redistribution of CLDN5 in leptomeningeal ECs, leakage of Sulfo-NHS-biotin, the increase in the area occupied by leptomeningeal vasculature, or the fractional increase in the number of ECs showing induction of the NF kappaB reporter (Figure 8B-D).
evidence: This is an observation from clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: Eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on leakage of Sulfo-NHS-biotin upon infection.
source: Surprisingly, eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the infection-dependent redistribution of CLDN5 in leptomeningeal ECs, leakage of Sulfo-NHS-biotin, the increase in the area occupied by leptomeningeal vasculature, or the fractional increase in the number of ECs showing induction of the NF kappaB reporter (Figure 8B-D).
evidence: This is an observation from clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: Eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the increase in the area occupied by leptomeningeal vasculature upon infection.
source: Surprisingly, eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the infection-dependent redistribution of CLDN5 in leptomeningeal ECs, leakage of Sulfo-NHS-biotin, the increase in the area occupied by leptomeningeal vasculature, or the fractional increase in the number of ECs showing induction of the NF kappaB reporter (Figure 8B-D).
evidence: This is an observation from clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the fractional increase in the number of ECs showing induction of the NF kappaB reporter upon infection.
source: Surprisingly, eliminating leptomeningeal macrophages had little or no effect on the infection-dependent redistribution of CLDN5 in leptomeningeal ECs, leakage of Sulfo-NHS-biotin, the increase in the area occupied by leptomeningeal vasculature, or the fractional increase in the number of ECs showing induction of the NF kappaB reporter (Figure 8B-D).
evidence: This is an observation from clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 8D.

claim: After clodronate depletion of CNS macrophages at P3, the number of macrophages in the leptomeninges at P6 increases only modestly following infection.
source: In support of the earlier inference that relatively few macrophages migrate into the leptomeninges 1 day after infection, the data in Figure 8C and D show that after clodronate depletion of CNS macrophages at P3, the number of macrophages in the leptomeninges at P6 increases only modestly following infection.
evidence: This is an observation from clodronate depletion experiments shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: LPS stimulation of TLR4 signaling plays a central role in the response of the leptomeningeal vasculature to infection (CLDN5 and PECAM1 redistribution, vessel swelling, and leakage).
source: Taken together, these experiments, together with the LPS treatment experiment (Figure 5A–C), show that (1) LPS stimulation of TLR4 signaling plays a central role in the response of the leptomeningeal vasculature to infection (CLDN5 and PECAM1 redistribution, vessel swelling, and leakage), and (2) this vascular response is largely independent of leptomeningeal macrophages, by far the most abundant immune cells in the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of LPS treatment, Tlr4-/- experiments, and macrophage depletion experiments.

claim: The vascular response to infection is largely independent of leptomeningeal macrophages.
source: Taken together, these experiments, together with the LPS treatment experiment (Figure 5A–C), show that (1) LPS stimulation of TLR4 signaling plays a central role in the response of the leptomeningeal vasculature to infection (CLDN5 and PECAM1 redistribution, vessel swelling, and leakage), and (2) this vascular response is largely independent of leptomeningeal macrophages, by far the most abundant immune cells in the leptomeninges.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of Ccr2-/- experiments and macrophage depletion experiments.

claim: At this age (P5-P6), the immaturity of the adaptive immune system and the rapidity of infection imply that the host response depends largely, and perhaps exclusively, on the innate immune system.
source: At this age, the immaturity of the adaptive immune system and the rapidity of infection imply that the host response depends largely, and perhaps exclusively, on the innate immune system.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about immune system development in neonatal mice.

claim: All of the major meningeal cell types – including ECs, macrophages, and fibroblasts – exhibit large and distinctive changes in their transcriptomes in response to bacterial infection.
source: In response to bacterial infection, all of the major meningeal cell types – including ECs, macrophages, and fibroblasts – exhibit large and distinctive changes in their transcriptomes.
evidence: This is a summary of the snRNAseq results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: ECs in leptomeningeal capillaries and veins lose nuclear LEF1 upon infection.
source: In addition, ECs in leptomeningeal capillaries redistribute CLDN5 and PECAM1, leptomeningeal capillaries become enlarged and disorganized and they exhibit foci of reduced BBB integrity, and ECs in leptomeningeal capillaries and veins lose nuclear LEF1.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5F and quantified in Figure 5H.

claim: Leptomeningeal capillaries become enlarged and disorganized upon infection.
source: In addition, ECs in leptomeningeal capillaries redistribute CLDN5 and PECAM1, leptomeningeal capillaries become enlarged and disorganized and they exhibit foci of reduced BBB integrity, and ECs in leptomeningeal capillaries and veins lose nuclear LEF1.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: This simple and robust model of bacterial meningitis in infancy should prove useful in dissecting mechanisms of pathophysiology.
source: This simple and robust model of bacterial meningitis in infancy should prove useful in dissecting mechanisms of pathophysiology.
evidence: This is speculation about the future utility of the model.

claim: The analyses focused on the response at 22 hr post-infection and earlier and later events have not been studied.
source: First, the analyses focused on the response at 22 hr post-infection and earlier and later events have not been studied.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: The movements, if any, of immune cells between compartments have not been studied.
source: Second, the movements, if any, of immune cells between compartments have not been studied, and therefore it is unclear whether some of the changes in transcriptome profiles should be ascribed to changes in cell state – that is the same cells as were present prior to infection, but with an altered transcriptional program – or the ingress of immune cells from non-meningeal pools.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Previous cell tracing analyses have shown that the pool of myeloid cells that supplies the meninges includes cells that are locally sequestered in the skull bones.
source: Interestingly, previous cell tracing analyses have shown that the pool of myeloid cells that supplies the meninges includes cells that are locally sequestered in the skull bones (Herisson et al., 2018; Cugurra et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The modest increases in macrophage density in the leptomeninges following infection imply a correspondingly modest influx of cells from non-meningeal reservoirs.
source: The modest increases in macrophage density in the leptomeninges following infection, with or without clodronate treatment (Figures 2E, 8C and D), imply a correspondingly modest influx of cells from non-meningeal reservoirs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed modest increases in macrophage density.

claim: Most of the transcriptomic changes are, at present, of unknown functional significance.
source: Third, most of the transcriptomic changes are, at present, of unknown functional significance, and, more specifically, the clinical significance of the observed cellular and molecular changes is also not clear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: Increases or decreases in the abundance of particular SLC transcripts imply corresponding changes in the transmembrane movement of a defined set of small molecules.
source: For example, increases or decreases in the abundance of particular SLC transcripts (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) imply corresponding changes in the transmembrane movement of a defined set of small molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of SLC transporters.

claim: Comparisons with previously published single cell (sc) RNAseq data from mouse meninges emphasize the challenges of correlating data from tissues harvested at different ages, prepared by different methods, and subject to undefined batch effects.
source: Comparisons with previously published single cell (sc) RNAseq data from mouse meninges emphasize the challenges of correlating data from tissues harvested at different ages, prepared by different methods, and subject to undefined batch effects.
evidence: This is a general observation about challenges in comparing scRNAseq datasets.

claim: The role of LPS in mediating BBB breakdown has been intensively studied, primarily in the context of the vasculature within the brain parenchyma.
source: The role of LPS in mediating BBB breakdown has been intensively studied, primarily in the context of the vasculature within the brain parenchyma (Wispelwey et al., 1988; Banks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the brain, LPS treatment leads to a reduction in EC tight junctions secondary to a decrease in tight junction protein abundance and changes in tight junction protein localization.
source: In the brain, LPS treatment leads to a reduction in EC tight junctions secondary to a decrease in tight junction protein abundance and changes in tight junction protein localization (Peng et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: In multiple cell types, TLR4 signaling (i.e. LPS-induced signaling) activates the NF-kappa B pathway.
source: In multiple cell types, TLR4 signaling (i.e. LPS-induced signaling) activates the NF-kappa B pathway, and that connection presumably accounts for the NF-kappa B reporter activation in meningeal ECs observed here.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TLR4 signaling.

claim: The altered localization of CLDN5 and the spatial correlation between this mis-localization and BBB disruption suggests that increased plasma membrane protein internalization and/or degradation could play a role in EC barrier defects.
source: Although the infection-induced down-regulation of transcripts coding for cell-cell junction proteins in ECs, arachnoid barrier cells, and other cell types did not reach statistical significance (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), the altered localization of CLDN5 and the spatial correlation between this mis-localization and BBB disruption (e.g. Figure 5A) suggests that increased plasma membrane protein internalization and/or degradation could play a role in EC barrier defects.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed CLDN5 mislocalization and BBB disruption.

claim: The NF-kappa B and WNT pathways can exhibit either positive and negative cross-regulation, depending on cell type and developmental context.
source: The NF-kappa B and WNT pathways can exhibit either positive and negative cross-regulation, depending on cell type and developmental context (Ma and Hottiger, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: IKKalpha phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN stabilization and increased WNT signaling.
source: By comparing BETA-CATENIN level, localization, and signaling in WT mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) and in MEFs homozygous for inactivating mutations in IKKalpha or IKKbeta (the inflammation-activated kinases that phosphorylate the inhibitory binding partner of NF kappaB, leading to NF kappaB activation), Lamberti et al., 2001 found that IKKalpha and IKKbeta phosphorylate BETA-CATENIN on different sites and with opposite effects. IKKalpha phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN stabilization and increased WNT signaling, whereas IKKbeta phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN destabilization and decreased WNT signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation (Lamberti et al., 2001).

claim: IKKbeta phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN destabilization and decreased WNT signaling.
source: By comparing BETA-CATENIN level, localization, and signaling in WT mouse embryo fibroblasts (MEFs) and in MEFs homozygous for inactivating mutations in IKKalpha or IKKbeta (the inflammation-activated kinases that phosphorylate the inhibitory binding partner of NF kappaB, leading to NF kappaB activation), Lamberti et al., 2001 found that IKKalpha and IKKbeta phosphorylate BETA-CATENIN on different sites and with opposite effects. IKKalpha phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN stabilization and increased WNT signaling, whereas IKKbeta phosphorylation leads to BETA-CATENIN destabilization and decreased WNT signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation (Lamberti et al., 2001).

claim: Reduced LEF1 in ECs in the infected leptomeninges could reflect BETA-CATENIN down-regulation via the activated NF kappaB pathway.
source: These precedents in other cell types suggest that reduced LEF1 – and presumably reduced canonical WNT signaling – in ECs in the infected leptomeninges could reflect BETA-CATENIN down-regulation via the activated NF kappaB pathway.
evidence: This is speculation based on established knowledge about NF-kappa B and WNT pathway interactions and the observed LEF1 reduction.

claim: Reduced canonical WNT signaling in ECs would be predicted to reduce BBB integrity.
source: Reduced canonical WNT signaling in ECs would be predicted to reduce BBB integrity (Rattner et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about WNT signaling in BBB maintenance, supported by a citation.

claim: The flat geometry of the meninges and its superficial location between the brain and the skull present unusually favorable opportunities for both in vitro and in vivo microscopy.
source: The flat geometry of the meninges and its superficial location between the brain and the skull present unusually favorable opportunities for both in vitro and in vivo microscopy.
evidence: This is a general observation about the anatomical advantages of the meninges for imaging.

claim: The relative thinness of the dissected mouse leptomeninges and dura provide excellent access to antibodies and also facilitate high quality confocal imaging without the need for chemical clearing agents.
source: For in vitro analyses, the relative thinness of the dissected mouse leptomeninges and dura provide excellent access to antibodies and also facilitate high quality confocal imaging without the need for chemical clearing agents, as described here.
evidence: This is an observation from the methods used in this study.

claim: Thinned skull preparations that permit two-photon imaging of the mouse meninges have been described.
source: In vivo, thinned skull preparations that permit two-photon imaging of the mouse meninges have been described, and this approach can be applied to mice with fluorescent immune cells that have been inoculated with fluorescent bacteria to allow single-cell resolution in vivo imaging of bacterial meningitis in a native context (Kjos et al., 2015; Coles et al., 2017b; Manglani and McGavern, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A largely unexplored opportunity exists for ex vivo culture and live imaging of the dissected leptomeninges and dura.
source: A largely unexplored opportunity also exists for ex vivo culture and live imaging of the dissected leptomeninges and dura (Glimcher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is speculation about future research opportunities, with a citation to a related method.

claim: Numerous gaps remain in our understanding of the pathophysiology of bacterial meningitis.
source: Despite decades of research, numerous gaps remain in our understanding of the pathophysiology of bacterial meningitis.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mouse models of meningitis, together with new technologies for interrogating these models, can provide insights that inform the understanding of human meningitis.
source: In each of these areas, mouse models of meningitis, together with new technologies for interrogating these models, can provide insights that inform the understanding of human meningitis.
evidence: This is speculation about the future utility of mouse models.
